items.title: It's Not an LLM, So What Does It Do? 3 Real Apps I built with Jev
items.description:
"Okay, you told me it's not an LLM. So what does it do?" That is the question I keep getting since the last video, and it is a fair one. So today, three apps I built. One sorts my YouTube comments into seven buckets in a few seconds. One grades a blog post while I type it. One decides which AI model should answer before a single token streams.

In this video I show three real apps built around a decision model, not a chat prompt. You will watch 100 YouTube comments land in seven buckets with a needs-reply flag, a blog draft graded on ten checks 900 ms after you stop typing, and a chat app that picks the model before the answer streams. For each app you see the UI first, then the one question behind it.

- How classification works: sort 100 real comments into seven buckets with a needs-reply flag in about a second
- How real-time feedback works: grade a draft on ten writing and SEO checks moments after you stop typing
- How model routing works: let the app pick cheap, balanced, or premium models based on the prompt
- Why a decision model fits these jobs better than sending full prompts to an LLM every time
- Three ideas you can adapt and build this week, in any language or framework

If you learned something new, leave a thumbs up, subscribe, and tell me in the comments what you would sort, grade, or route.

items.title: The Hugging Face Attack Was Bigger Than We Thought - Ajeya Cotra
The Dark Arts of Skill Engineering — Paul Bakaus, Renaissance Geek (Impeccable)
items.description:
Paul Bakaus once turned the entire web orange. He wrote jQuery UI, shipped an orange default theme, assumed people would change it, and watched them not. So when he points out that the purple gradients everyone learned to mock came from a CSS framework's default sample page, and that AI generated design now has its own house shade of beige, he speaks as the cause rather than the critic. That history is what makes his central claim land. A ban does not produce originality, it relocates the model one cluster over: forbid one overused font and it reaches for the next nearest thing in latent space. Slop is a moving target. The median is the model's gravity, and a few hundred lines of carefully written prose cannot pull against it.

So he stopped treating a skill as a packaged prompt and started treating it as an extension of the harness, which is what this workshop is really about. Nine techniques, each aimed at something prose cannot do. Two sub agents kept blind to each other, one playing design director and one running a deterministic linter, because a single thread grading its own work always says it did well. Naming your top three fonts and then throwing all three away to shave off the safe prediction. A script whose only job is to hand the model a random seed it could not have guessed. Instructions emitted on standard output rather than buried in prose, which models follow far more reliably, at the cost of prompt caching. Hooks that block a write instead of complaining afterward. And the discipline underneath all of it: if a gate can be skipped, it will be.

items.title: Spring Office Hours: S5E24 - Jev, Java and Spring
items.description:
Jev is a new model from TypeSafe that answers typed questions about your content. You send it some text and the decisions you need. It returns a probability, a choice, or a score instead of a paragraph. That makes it a natural fit for the decisions your code already has to make. Is this ticket urgent? Which team should own it? Which model should answer this prompt?

In this episode, Dan and DaShaun talk about why this matters for Java and Spring developers. Most of us have been asking a chat model to make a decision and then parsing prose to get the answer out. Jev gives you a typed answer you can branch on, with a confidence you can check. Dan shares what he learned getting it running in Java and Spring Boot, and the two of them talk through where a decision model fits next to Spring AI and where it does not.

Then it is your turn. Bring your questions about Jev, Spring Boot 4, Spring AI, or anything else in the Spring ecosystem. We will answer them live.

items.title: How Spring Boot 4 Starters Actually Work (I Built One for Jev)
items.description:
This controller asks for a JevClient and Spring Boot just hands it one. I never wrote a bean for it. No enable annotation, no config class, no component scan. So where did it come from? From a starter I built this week, and we are going to open it up file by file.

Last week I built a Jev client Spring Boot: a RestClient, a few records, and a properties class. This week I turn all of that into a Spring Boot 4 starter. You add one dependency, set one environment variable, inject JevClient, and get three typed answers back. Then we open the starter file by file so you can see exactly how auto-configuration, conditions, properties, and the imports file make every starter work.

- What a Spring Boot starter really is: defaults and wiring you get for free until you override them
- How auto-configuration works, from the AutoConfiguration.imports file to conditional beans
- How the starter clones Boot's RestClient.Builder so your timeouts and converters carry over
- How to install a local starter with mvnw clean install and use it in a fresh Boot 4 app
- How to inject JevClient and ask urgent (noul), team (choice), and severity (score) questions

If you learned something new, leave a thumbs up, subscribe to the channel, and drop a comment with what you would build with Jev. Happy coding.

items.title: Why Information Has a Price in Intelligence - Alexander Mattick
items.description:
Alexander Mattick is a researcher at Fraunhofer IIS and a PhD researcher at the University of Technology Nuremberg (UTN), and a regular on Yannic Kilcher's Discord. He first came on MLST in 2022, after helping research the Yann LeCun and Randall Balestriero episode on interpolation.

SPONSOR:
---
Cyber Fund built the Monastery to help founders ship products that were impossible a year ago. Applications for Batch 1 are now open.
Apply now: https://cyber.fund
---

Alexander treats inference as the thread running through modern machine learning: once you have a model, what does it cost to get an answer out of it? He works through Monte Carlo, GFlowNets, energy-based models, diffusion, normalising flows and flow matching, with four short explainers he recorded himself. He is blunt about energy-based models: you can sample from them in principle, but it is rarely worth the compute. JEPA and "world model", he says, are closer to branding than to technical categories.

The second half covers theories of deep learning, none of which he thinks predicts enough yet to guide practice, then reinforcement learning. Against "Reward is Enough" and the Bitter Lesson he argues that real-world information is expensive, so constraints are the cheapest way to give a system what experts already know. He also explains why prediction is not control, and why a robot demo says little about how often the robot fails.

---

items.title: Tap to Pay - 72x More Complicated Than a Simple Tap! 💳📡
items.description:
Expand your knowledge!  Go to http://brilliant.org/BranchEducation/ for a 30-day free trial and expand your knowledge. Use this link to get a 20% discount on their annual premium membership.

Tap to pay, or contactless payment, seems simple: you hold your credit card over the terminal, and a second later the screen says approved. But it's a lot more complicated than that!! The card has no battery or wires, and feels like just a solid piece of plastic. So how does it power up, talk to the terminal, and prove it isn't a fraudulent card — and all in less than a second!

In this video, we slow that one second way down and explore the physics and engineering behind wireless payments. We'll show you what's inside the payment terminal and your credit card, explain how a 13.56 MHz magnetic field powers the card, show how the two send data back and forth using amplitude and load modulation, and unpack the cryptography that keeps contactless payments secure. Then we branch out into tap to pay in smartphones, wireless payments with hotel key cards and ID badges, and the wider world of RFID.

Rust futures can feel mysterious, but the underlying machinery becomes much easier to understand when you build it yourself. In this deep dive, we explore how futures, polling, wakers, and pinning work together to power asynchronous Rust.

Chapters:
1:05 What is a Future?
2:35 Async Functions and State Machines
4:10 Polling: Pending and Ready
6:00 Wakers and Task Scheduling
7:55 Pinning in Rust
9:45 Building a Simple Executor

items.title: What's New in JDK 27: A Quick Feature Tour
items.description:
A quick tour of the JDK 27 OpenJDK project page. G1 as the default garbage collector, post-quantum key exchange for TLS 1.3, lazy constants, primitive types in pattern matching, and more. Read the JEPs to see why each decision was made.
#Java #JDK27 #OpenJDK #Programming #JavaDeveloper

items.title: Project Loom Explained in 3 JEPs
items.description:
Project Loom comes down to three JEPs. Virtual threads went final in JDK 21. Scope values went final in JDK 25. Structured concurrency groups tasks as one unit with one scope and one lifetime, so they finish or fail together.

#Java #ProjectLoom #StructuredConcurrency #VirtualThreads #JDK25

items.title: Is AI Killing the Next Generation of Engineers?
items.description:
What happens when AI takes over incident response?

Senior engineers build expertise through scar tissue from real production fires. If AI resolves every incident automatically, that feedback loop breaks - and skills atrophy fast.

🔗 Alex Palcuie breaks down the hidden cost of AI reliability tooling: https://bit.ly/4iEn9Hs 

#AI #SRE #DevOps #Reliability #InfoQ
